titleStmt.title: Visions in the Machine: Automated Tagging of the William Blake Archive

dhq:authorInfo.dhq:affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, North Carolina State University

dhq:bio.p: Grant Glass is an Adjunct Faculty member at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill School of Data Science and Society, a lecturer at North Carolina State University, and a Data Scientist at NetApp. Trained as a humanist, his research focuses on the intersection of computational linguistics, artificial intelligence, and the digital humanities. His recent work explores the computational analysis of cultural transmission and literary evolution across Robinson Crusoe texts. He is the technical editor at the William Blake Archive.

dhq:abstract.p: This paper investigates how multimodal AI can support — not replace — scholarly description of William Blake’s visual art. Using the William Blake Archive as a foundation, I develop a conceptual framework that distinguishes three levels of visual analysis (pattern recognition, motif identification, and iconographic interpretation) and use it to evaluate a working retrieval prototype built on Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) embeddings and Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) indexing over a 200-work stratified corpus. The paper defends three claims. First, that AI-assisted tagging is best understood as retrieval support rather than automated interpretation: it surfaces candidate matches that scholars then validate. Second, that performance degrades predictably across the three tiers: strong at object-level detection, moderate at motif-level pattern recognition, weak at Blake-specific iconography, and that this gradient is itself a useful empirical finding for archives weighing adoption. Third, that the responsible integration of AI tags into an existing scholarly archive requires explicit provenance, confidence scoring, human-in-the-loop validation, and audit logging, and that these requirements can be operationalized concretely. The paper does not claim to automate iconographic interpretation, to provide ground-truth identifications, or to generalize beyond the 200-work pilot; results should be read as alignment with the Archive’s descriptive practice on a stratified sample, not as validated interpretation. The contribution is a conceptual framework, a tested prototype, and an integration design that other archives confronting dense symbolic corpora can adapt.

div.head: 1. Introduction: The Challenge of Blake’s Visions and the Promise of AI
div.p: William Blake (1757-1827) remains a singular figure in the annals of art and literature, a poet, painter, and printmaker whose work defies easy categorization. Operating primarily outside the mainstream artistic conventions of his time, Blake forged a unique visual and textual language to explore profound themes of spirituality, mythology, politics, and the human psyche . His art is characterized by an idiosyncratic blend of influences, drawing on yet radically transforming biblical narratives, Miltonic epic, Neoclassical forms, and Gothic sensibilities . The result is a body of work marked by its visionary intensity and interpretive depth. Central to the challenge of engaging with Blake’s visual art is its characteristic complexity. His compositions are often densely populated with figures, interwoven with text, and structured according to symbolic rather than naturalistic principles. Blake developed a personal mythology populated by figures like Urizen (representing reason and law), Los (imagination and time), and Orc (rebellion and energy), whose meanings can shift across different works and contexts . This intricate symbolism, combined with his distinctive linear style and unconventional use of space, demands careful and informed interpretation.

One prime example of this complexity is The Vision of the Last Judgement. Extant in several versions and known primarily through detailed descriptions, this monumental conception presents a swirling vortex of figures that embody Blake’s intricate cosmology and eschatology . Its sheer density, symbolic richness, and variations across related works pose significant analytical challenges for traditional art-historical methods, making it a compelling test case for the potential application of computational techniques . The study of Blake has been revolutionized by the William Blake Archive (the Archive), a landmark digital humanities project launched in the mid-1990s . The Archive provides unprecedented access to high-resolution digital reproductions of Blake’s vast and widely dispersed works, including illuminated books, paintings, drawings, manuscripts, and commercial engravings. Its primary goal has been to establish a scholarly electronic edition, reuniting works scattered across global collections and providing detailed bibliographic, historical, and descriptive information for each object .

Beyond serving as a digital repository, the Archive represents a structured dataset of significant potential for computational analysis. It meticulously documents provenance, physical characteristics, and relationships between different states or versions of works, accompanied by extensive textual transcriptions and scholarly descriptions. This digital infrastructure, while primarily designed for scholarly access and textual scholarship, offers a foundation upon which new computational methods, including those from artificial intelligence (AI), might be built to explore Blake’s visual art in novel ways
.

It is crucial to distinguish among three levels of visual analysis to structure this investigation. At the most basic level, computer vision systems engage in pattern recognition, detecting edges, textures, shapes, and colors in pixel data. The Archive, however, operates at the motif level, recording that a particular visual pattern represents a tree or figure rather than documenting its specific visual characteristics. Beyond this lies symbolic interpretation, understanding that a tree might represent the Tree of Life or natural innocence in Blake’s mythology. This paper focuses primarily on how AI can bridge the gap between pattern recognition and motif identification, while acknowledging that symbolic interpretation remains fundamentally a humanistic endeavor.

div.head: 1.1 Scope and Contributions
div.p: This paper makes three distinct contributions at different levels of completion:

list.item: A conceptual framework for understanding how AI can bridge pattern recognition and motif identification within established archival practices, distinguishing what machines can reliably detect from what requires human judgment.

A functional retrieval prototype demonstrating sub-millisecond similarity search across a 200-work corpus representing Blake’s artistic range, with quantitative evaluation across three tiers of tagging complexity.

An exploratory case study applying iterative analytical methods to The Vision of the Last Judgement, demonstrating how regionally-balanced, source-weighted taxonomies can enhance motif detection in densely symbolic compositions.

div.p: I would like to pause here and state what this paper does not claim. To set clear expectations for a topic that invites overstatement, I explicitly state the boundaries of these contributions. This study investigates retrieval support, not automated interpretation. The system suggests candidate tags and visually similar works; it does not determine which figure is Urizen, decide what a given composition's serpent symbolizes, or produce iconographic readings. Where I report quantitative performance, I read those numbers as alignment with the Archive’s existing descriptive practice on a stratified 200-work sample, not as a ground-truth interpretation of Blake. The case study of The Vision of the Last Judgement demonstrates how iterative computational passes can support a scholar’s analysis of a single dense composition; it does not validate the method across Blake’s full oeuvre. Generalization beyond the pilot would require multi-annotator ground truth, external expert review, and corpus-wide scaling tests that are out of scope here.

I frame this work as a pilot study: a proof-of-concept that establishes feasibility for a clearly bounded retrieval task, rather than a production system for the full Archive. The 200-work corpus was stratified from 715 works available in the Archive to represent diversity across Blake’s oeuvre while remaining tractable for intensive methodological development; the rationale for that sample size, and the kinds of works it cannot yet speak to, are discussed in Section 6.2 and revisited under Limitations.

div.head: 1.2 Operational Definition of Tagging
div.p: Throughout this paper, tagging refers to the computational process of associating image regions or whole images with descriptive labels from a defined vocabulary. I distinguish three levels of tagging complexity:

list.item: Object-level tagging identifies concrete visual elements (serpent, book, human figure) without interpretive claims about their meaning.
Motif-level tagging identifies compositional patterns and conventional postures (outstretched arms, ascending figure, vortex composition) that recur across Blake’s work.
Iconographic tagging assigns Blake-specific identifications (Urizen, Los, Last Judgement throne) that require contextual knowledge of his mythology.

div.p: This hierarchy corresponds to increasing interpretive demands: object-level tagging lies closest to pattern recognition, while iconographic tagging approaches interpretation. Our pilot implementation demonstrates feasibility across all three levels and confirms that performance degrades as tagging approaches the interpretation stage, with significant implications for human-AI collaboration in digital art history.

div.head: 1.3 Research Questions
div.p: This paper addresses the following core research question:

How can current AI techniques assist scholars in the identification and cataloging of visual motifs within William Blake’s paintings by automating the translation from visual patterns to motif labels, and how can this pattern-to-motif mapping be integrated with the existing descriptive infrastructure of the William Blake Archive?

div.head: 1.4 Implications for Scholarly Practice
div.p: If successfully developed and validated, AI-assisted tagging would open three currently impractical lines of inquiry. Scholars could trace the frequency and evolution of specific visual elements, such as the serpent motif, across Blake’s entire oeuvre at a scale manual cataloging cannot reach, revealing patterns invisible to inspection of single works. Similarity search could surface unexpected visual affinities, linking, say, a figure in the Job illustrations to a compositionally similar figure in the Dante series and prompting comparative analyses that would not otherwise be initiated. And for works existing in multiple states or copies, automated comparison could highlight systematic variations in Blake’s treatment of specific elements across versions. None of these capabilities replaces interpretive scholarship; they redirect it from exhaustive cataloging (which the system can assist) toward interpretive synthesis (which remains human work).

This shift raises new responsibilities for archives: how to present AI-generated tags alongside human descriptions, how to indicate confidence levels, and how to prevent algorithmic suggestions from foreclosing interpretive possibilities rather than opening them. This inquiry is inherently interdisciplinary, situated at the intersection of art history, digital humanities, and computer science . It seeks to bridge the gap between the nuanced interpretive methods of art history and the pattern-recognition capabilities of AI, exploring both the potential synergies and the inherent limitations of applying computational tools to such complex and symbolically rich visual material.

div.head: 2. The William Blake Archive: Structure, Data, and Current Practices
div.p: The William Blake Archive is built upon a robust technical architecture designed to manage and present a large, complex corpus of digital objects and associated metadata (eaves_etal2019). While specific technical details evolve, its foundation involves standard digital library technologies and adherence to metadata standards common in digital humanities. Works are meticulously cataloged with unique identifiers, enabling precise referencing. Crucially, the Archive model accommodates the complex relationships inherent in Blake’s output, such as linking different copies of illuminated books (which Blake produced individually, leading to variations) or relating preliminary sketches to finished works.

Metadata standards play a key role. The Archive utilizes the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) guidelines for encoding Blake’s texts, ensuring scholarly rigor and interoperability . While TEI is primarily text-focused, the Archive also incorporates extensive metadata about the visual works themselves, covering aspects like medium, dimensions, support, date, and provenance. The Archive uses XML extensively, employing a primary Document Type Definition (DTD) known as the Blake Archive Description (BAD) for encoding texts, bibliographic commentary, and illustration descriptions, while TEI is used for other materials, such as bibliographies, where physical artifact description is not central . For instance, the multiple descriptions and potential lost versions of The Vision of the Last Judgement necessitate a structure capable of handling such complex interrelations. Understanding this underlying data model is crucial for assessing how visual information is represented and whether it can be readily extracted for AI purposes.

The Archive provides detailed scholarly descriptions for many of its objects. Examining the entry for a complex work like the Petworth House version of The Vision of the Last Judgement reveals the nature of current practices. Descriptions are typically narrative and interpretive, written by experts to guide understanding . They often identify key figures, explain the overall scene, discuss symbolism, and relate the work to Blake’s writings or other compositions. Fields like Description or potentially Objects Represented contain this information, often in free-text prose.

The vocabulary used in these descriptions is scholarly and interpretive, not necessarily a controlled vocabulary designed for machine processing. While terms might be consistent within a single description or by a single cataloger, variations in terminology across the entire archive are likely. Consistency depends heavily on editorial oversight and the specific cataloging guidelines employed over the project’s long history . Furthermore, the granularity of existing descriptions varies. They excel at providing a holistic interpretation of the scene but may not systematically list every single figure, object, or motif depicted. The focus is often on salient or symbolically important elements rather than exhaustive visual inventory. Annotations directly linking specific parts of the image to descriptive text are generally absent.

div.head: 2.1 Strengths and Limitations as AI Training Data
div.p: The Archive offers significant strengths as a potential data source for AI-driven analysis of Blake’s art. It provides access to a large corpus of high-resolution images, essential for training deep learning models . The images are accompanied by rich contextual metadata, including detailed provenance, dating, and relationships to other works, which could potentially inform AI analysis. Furthermore, the extensive textual descriptions and transcriptions associated with many images offer a valuable resource, particularly for multimodal AI approaches .

However, the Archive also presents limitations when considered as a direct source of training data for standard computer vision tasks. The primary challenge lies in the nature of the visual annotations. Visual descriptions are typically narrative and interpretive rather than structured lists of labels suitable for supervised learning . There may be inconsistencies in terminology and granularity across the archive. Crucially, the lack of fine-grained annotations, such as bounding boxes or segmentation masks, which specify the location and extent of objects within the image, poses a significant hurdle for training object detection or segmentation models .

This assessment points towards a structural characteristic of the archive: Its origins and primary goals centered on scholarly access, textual encoding (TEI usage), and comprehensive bibliographic and historical metadata likely result in textual data being far more structured and consistent than visual metadata from an AI perspective. Visual description, while rich, follows humanistic interpretive conventions rather than the systematic tagging protocols ideal for machine learning .

div.head: 2.2 The Archive’s Editorial Stance
div.p: The William Blake Archive maintains a deliberately restrained approach to interpretation, focusing on descriptive documentation that aims for scholarly objectivity. As the Archive’s editors note, illustration descriptions are descriptive, as objective as possible, even if true objectivity is not possible. The Archive engages in limited interpretation, such as labeling a figure as Urizen, but avoids deep symbolic analysis. This approach provides the ground for rigorous interpretation, much as a letterpress text provides the ground for literary interpretation. This philosophy has important implications for AI integration. The Archive records the representation of motifs, not patterns. When a human cataloger identifies a tree in Blake’s work, they are making an interpretive leap from a specific visual pattern to a conceptual category that encompasses infinite possible visual instantiations. No two trees in Blake’s art, or in nature, share the same pattern, yet humans readily group these diverse patterns under the single motif label tree. This many-to-one mapping from patterns to motifs represents a fundamental challenge for computational approaches.

div.head: 3.1 Blake’s Iconographic System
div.p: A vast body of art historical scholarship is dedicated to deciphering William Blake’s complex and deeply personal iconography. Blake constructed a unique mythological system populated by figures such as Urizen (representing reason and law), Los (imagination and time), Orc (rebellion and energy), Enitharmon (spiritual beauty and female counterpart to Los), and many others (damon, 1965). These figures are not static allegories but dynamic entities whose significance can evolve throughout Blake’s career and vary depending on the specific context of a work .

Key symbols of the serpent, compasses, flames, lilies, and anvils all recur throughout his oeuvre, imbued with layers of meaning drawn from biblical, Miltonic, Neoplatonic, alchemical, and contemporary political sources, all refracted through Blake’s unique visionary lens . Blake’s relationship with existing traditions was one of radical transformation. He engaged deeply with the Bible and the works of John Milton but reinterpreted them according to his own spiritual and political vision, often inverting traditional meanings . Similarly, while employing elements of Neoclassical linearity and Gothic energy, his style ultimately served his internal vision rather than adhering strictly to contemporary aesthetic norms . This synthesis of diverse sources into a highly personal symbolic language creates significant interpretive challenges. Meanings are often polysemous (having multiple interpretations), ambiguous, and resistant to straightforward decoding. Understanding Blake’s symbolism requires familiarity not only with his visual works but also with his poetry and prophetic writings, where these concepts are further elaborated .

div.head: 3.2 Recurring Visual Motifs
div.p: Beyond specific symbols and named figures, Blake’s visual art is characterized by recurring visual motifs, postures, gestures, and compositional structures . Figures with dramatically outstretched arms, bodies bent in despair or constricted by bonds, dynamic vortex compositions suggesting spiritual energy or chaos, and layered planes creating a sense of shallow, stage-like space are common features. Blake’s distinctive style emphasizes strong contour lines, flattened perspective, and a powerful, often idealized or exaggerated, rendering of the human form . A key element of his visual strategy, particularly in the illuminated books, is the integration of text and image. Text does not merely caption the image, nor does the image simply illustrate the text; rather, they interact in complex ways, often weaving together on the page, with decorative elements blurring the lines between writing and drawing . These recurring visual elements and stylistic choices are not merely decorative; they are integral to the works’ meaning and affective power, conveying states of being, spiritual struggles, and cosmic events through a consistent, albeit evolving, visual vocabulary .

div.head: 3.3 The Vision of the Last Judgement as Test Case
div.p: The Vision of the Last Judgement serves as an exemplary case study of Blake’s complexity . Known through several related works and detailed descriptions by Blake himself, the composition depicts a vast panorama of humanity rising to judgment or falling into damnation, presided over by Christ enthroned on the Mercy Seat, surrounded by apostles and heavenly figures. Below, the Book of Life is opened, Satan is wrapped in the Serpent’s coils, and figures representing various states of salvation and damnation populate the scene. The composition is dense, dynamic, and spatially complex, drawing heavily on traditional Last Judgement iconography but reinterpreted through Blake’s personal mythology .

Identifying specific figures requires knowledge of both biblical tradition and Blake’s own symbolic system . Distinguishing between numerous nude or semi-nude figures based on subtle postural differences or their position within the overall symbolic program is challenging. Interpreting the relationships between figures — for example, the complex interplay between judgment, mercy, and the creative imagination — requires deep engagement with Blake’s thought . Specific elements, like the precise identity of allegorical figures representing states of sin or redemption, or the exact meaning of certain gestures, remain subjects of scholarly debate .

Each of the demands set out above, from recognizing context-dependent symbols to distinguishing members of Blake's personal pantheon by subtle attributes, to parsing densely overlapping figures in compositions like The Vision of the Last Judgment, represents a different kind of computational challenge. Each of these concerns has been engaged to varying degrees by different strands of the technical literature. Computational iconography has begun to handle motif-level recognition for artists with shared conventional vocabularies but has largely avoided artists with idiosyncratic personal mythologies. Multimodal vision-language models have made flexible, prompt-based retrieval newly feasible for small-corpus archives. Similarity-retrieval infrastructure has matured to the point where latency and scale are no longer the constraints they once were. And the digital-humanities literature on AI evaluation has supplied the vocabulary needed to ask of any such system what it is doing, on whose behalf, and against what standard. The next section surveys these four conversations in turn, to locate precisely where the present paper enters them — and where it does not.

div.head: 4. Related Work: AI, Computer Vision, and Cultural Heritage
div.p: Related work falls into four conversations that this paper joins: computational iconography and motif recognition in art history; multimodal vision-language models applied to cultural heritage; similarity retrieval over art image collections; and the digital-humanities literature on critical evaluation and bias in AI-assisted scholarship. Treating them together makes this paper's contribution easier to locate. The paper is the first, to my knowledge, to bring all four to bear on an artist with a dense personal mythology, and to do so under a framework that explicitly distinguishes what a computational system supports (retrieval) from what it does not (interpretation).

The four conversations are also a useful diagnostic for why Blake has remained outside the main computational-art-history literature to date. Each conversation handles part of what a Blake-scale tagging project would need; none has yet had to address them all at once.

div.head: 4.1 Computational Iconography and Motif Recognition
div.p: The computational analysis of art-historical imagery has matured rapidly over the last decade. Foundational work by established visual search over painting collections, demonstrating that off-the-shelf object detectors trained on natural photographs could transfer, with caveats, to artistic imagery. Subsequent work extended this into explicitly iconographic territory: released a dataset and convolutional model for iconography classification in paintings, and pushed the problem toward large-scale hierarchical classification, demonstrating that structured label spaces can substantially improve performance over flat classifiers. provide an instructive model from an adjacent problem space: Their art-historical pose dataset required iterative refinement of annotation guidelines and quality-controlled multi-annotator review. Their work addresses pose estimation across a multi-collection dataset and does not engage with the Archive directly; I cite it here as a procedural template for how annotation guidelines could be developed if and when the Archive’s curatorial team chose to extend descriptive metadata in this direction.

These projects share a common architecture. They start with a labelled corpus (often built with substantial editorial labour), train or fine-tune a deep model on that corpus, and report accuracy on held-out subsets. Their typical objects of study are stylistic or attributional or, in the iconographic case, drawn from broadly shared visual vocabularies such as saints, biblical scenes, and classical motifs whose iconographic conventions are stable across centuries and across many artists. The general-purpose computer-vision toolkit they draw on: convolutional architectures such as ResNet , detection frameworks such as Faster R-CNN and Mask R-CNN , and Vision Transformers (dosovitskiy, 2020). All of these techniques have been extended further by end-to-end detection models and by general-purpose segmentation systems such as Segment Anything .

Three reasons explain why these methods have largely avoided artists with dense personal iconographies like Blake. First, the data requirement: A personal symbolic system requires not just images but extensive scholarly annotation that links visual features to specific meanings, and that annotation does not yet exist at the scale supervised methods need. Second, the evaluation problem: Standard accuracy metrics measure pattern-matching against a ground truth, but a meaningful Blake iconographic identification typically depends on context, on inter-textual evidence, and on contested scholarly judgment that no single ground truth captures . Third, the interpretive problem: An artist whose imagery deliberately resists conventional iconography is precisely the artist for whom automated interpretation is least likely to succeed. The present paper does not attempt to remove these obstacles. It accepts them and proposes a framework in which AI supports retrieval and surfaces candidate matches that scholars validate, rather than producing iconographic readings directly.

div.head: 4.2 Multimodal Vision-Language Models and Cultural Heritage
div.p: The most consequential recent shift in computer vision for cultural-heritage applications has been the emergence of multimodal vision-language models. CLIP [Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training] and BLIP place images and natural-language text into a shared embedding space, allowing flexible retrieval and zero-shot classification without task-specific training. The practical effect is that art-historical applications no longer require a fully labelled dataset before useful experiments can begin: A researcher can write a tag prompt in plain English and retrieve candidate matches against an embedding index of an entire collection.

frame the broader claim that digital art history has matured beyond the digitization phase into a computationally distinct discipline, in part because multimodal models such as CLIP can reveal visual relationships across large corpora that resist manual analysis. The methodological turn this paper joins, then, has two features. Earlier supervised approaches surveyed by treated the labelled dataset as a prerequisite for analysis; the multimodal turn treats the prompt as the unit of investigation and the embedding as the substrate. This shift is particularly consequential for archives like the William Blake Archive, where the labor required to assemble a supervised dataset at scale has been the principal barrier to computational analysis.

To tailor a pre-trained model to a specific artist or lexicon, researchers continue to rely on adaptation methods suited for limited labeled data, including transfer learning , few-shot learning , and weakly supervised techniques . The implementation reported in this paper uses zero-shot CLIP with no fine-tuning, partly because the Archive does not yet provide labels in a form suitable for supervised training, and partly because zero-shot retrieval is precisely the operation the paper's contribution is designed to support. The trade-offs between zero-shot and fine-tuned configurations are discussed methodologically in Section 6.1.

div.head: 4.3 Similarity Retrieval Over Art Image Collections
div.p: The third conversation this paper joins is the technical literature on similarity retrieval in art collections. demonstrated visual link retrieval across painting databases, showing that learned visual features could surface non-obvious compositional relationships among works in large heterogeneous corpora. and colleagues (2020) report the related ImageCLEF retrieval benchmarks that have set the practical standard for cross-domain image retrieval evaluation. On the indexing side, the FAISS library has made it routine to deploy sub-millisecond similarity search over millions of high-dimensional embeddings; for collections in the hundreds or low thousands of works typical of single-artist archives, retrieval latency has ceased to be a meaningful constraint.

More recent work on open-vocabulary detection closes part of the gap between similarity retrieval and tag-level identification, allowing systems to localize objects within an image based on natural-language prompts. The retrieval prototype in Section 6.3 of this paper draws on this lineage technically, CLIP embeddings indexed by FAISS and conceptually: The contribution is positioned as retrieval support, not as a novel detection architecture. What is new is the application to an artist whose iconographic vocabulary is unusually personal and unusually dense, and the explicit framing of retrieval support as the appropriate level of computational assistance for that case.

div.head: 4.4 Critical Evaluation and Bias in AI-Assisted Scholarship
div.p: The fourth conversation is the digital-humanities literature on what AI does to scholarship when it is brought into it, and on what scholars should ask of computational tools before accepting their outputs. Crawford's (2021) account of the political economy of AI systems and Foka, Huvila, Westin, and Sanchez Bueno's (2025) analysis of the bias loop in cultural-heritage ML pipelines both name the same problem from different angles: biases embedded in historical collection practices (what was preserved, described, and prioritized) are encoded into training data, amplified by model behavior, and then naturalized by deployment into archive interfaces . The Archive's own descriptive practice is not exempt from this loop, and any computational system trained on or evaluated against its descriptions inherits the priorities of its editorial history. Section 6.5 returns to this point as an evaluation-circularity disclosure.

On the evaluation side, provides the standard reference for precision, recall, F-measure, and the conditions under which each is appropriate; this paper relies on Powers's framing in Section 6.5 when reporting tier-stratified performance. anticipated many of the cross-disciplinary tensions that still shape evaluation: Art historians and computer scientists tend to disagree about what a successful identification looks like, about how much interpretive content a tag should carry, and about what counts as a fair test case. The three-tier framework adopted in this paper (Section 1) is partly a response to Spratt's and Elgammal’s observation: By distinguishing object-level, motif-level, and iconographic-level tags, the framework makes the evaluation appropriate to the claim and makes the system's limits visible to readers from both disciplines.

div.head: 4.5 What This Paper Adds
div.p: Across these four conversations, the present paper is positioned not as a technical demonstration but as a digital-humanities argument. It accepts that computational iconography has not yet engaged Blake, that the multimodal turn lowers the barrier to entry, that similarity retrieval is now technically routine at this scale, and that critical evaluation must remain central. Its contribution is to bring those four points together under a single framework: the three-tier distinction between pattern, motif, and iconographic interpretation, and to test that framework on a 200-work stratified Blake corpus.

Three things follow from that positioning. First, the paper does not claim to extend the state of the art in computer vision; the technical components (CLIP, FAISS, PCA visualization) are standard and intentionally so. Second, the paper does claim that applying those standard components to a corpus this iconographically demanding, under a framework that explicitly bounds what the system can do, yields findings that are useful to other archives confronting similar problems, most concretely, a measurable performance gradient across the three tiers and a concrete integration plan (Section 7) for AI-suggested tags alongside human descriptive scholarship. Third, the paper claims that the specifically humanities-side contribution, the framework, the integration plan, and the set of success criteria specified in Section 8, is the part most worth carrying forward to artists and corpora beyond Blake.

div.head: 5. Data and Annotation in the Archive
div.p: Section 4 surveyed the technical literature on computer vision, multimodal models, similarity retrieval, and critical evaluation. The question now is operational: What does the William Blake Archive specifically provide, what does it not provide, and what follows for how a computational system can be built on top of it? This section is deliberately narrow. It does not restate general requirements for training computer vision models; those are already in the literature cited and would only duplicate Section 4. Instead, it maps the Archive's existing data against the analytical requirements established there, identifies the gaps that matter for this study, and sets up the methodological choices made in Section 6.

div.head: 5.1 Mapping the Archive Against Analytical Requirements
div.p: The Archive's principal strength as a data source is the combination of image quality and scholarly description: High-resolution images of roughly 715 fully digitized works are paired with TEI-encoded textual descriptions written by Blake specialists over three decades of editorial work . For zero-shot retrieval against a pre-trained multimodal embedding model (as in Section 6), image volume and quality are not binding constraints. The binding constraints are in the label structure, not in the images.

table.head: Blake Archive Data vs. AI Training Requirements: Mapping the William Blake Archive's existing data against the requirements of common computational analyses. The image-side of the Archive comfortably exceeds current model requirements; the operational gaps are concentrated on the label side.

div.head: 5.2 The Label-Side Gap
div.p: Four interrelated gaps shape what is and is not possible at present. The Archive does not currently provide bounding boxes or segmentation masks of the kind that object-detection and segmentation models require. Scholarly descriptions use varied terminology for the same concept, such as serpent, snake, and Satan-Serpent" which appear across descriptions as the cataloger's reading of a given figure shifts, and thus require substantial normalization before they can serve as supervised labels. Descriptions tend to characterize overall interpretation rather than exhaustively list every identifiable element, because that is what the Archive's editorial practice rightly prioritizes. And coverage is uneven across the corpus, with richly described works sitting alongside minimally annotated ones, reflecting the Archive's longstanding decision to prioritize editorial depth over uniform annotation.

The first two of these gaps are addressable by editorial labor and controlled vocabulary; they describe missing infrastructure, not missing scholarship. The second two are constitutive features of the Archive's mission and should not be fixed so much as worked with. Exhaustive labeling of every figure and object in every work was never the Archive's purpose, and a computational system that requires such labeling is asking the wrong thing of the Archive. A system that supports scholarly retrieval by surfacing candidate matches and leaving interpretation to the scholar does not need exhaustive supervised labels in the first place.

div.head: 5.3 Implications for Method
div.p: Three methodological choices follow directly from the data state described above and govern the implementation in Section 6. First, the system is built on zero-shot multimodal embeddings rather than supervised classifiers, because the Archive's current labels do not support supervised training at scale. Second, evaluation is framed as alignment with the Archive's existing descriptive practice on a stratified sample, rather than as validation against an external ground truth; the Archive's descriptions are the most authoritative reference available, and any computational system trained on or evaluated against them inherits the priorities of its editorial history, a circularity disclosed in Section 6.5. Third, the three-tier framework introduced in Section 1 (object-level, motif-level, iconographic-level) is partly a response to the granularity gap described in Table 1: By matching the evidentiary burden to the kind of tag being produced, the framework makes the system's performance interpretable even where the underlying labels are uneven.

div.head: 6.1 Methods At A Glance
div.p: For readers approaching this study from a humanities background, the technical vocabulary in this section can be reduced to five working terms. CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training) is a neural model that places images and text into a shared vector space so that semantically related items lie near one another. An embedding is the coordinate of an item in that space. For this study, an embedding is a 512-dimensional vector summarizing what a model has learned to associate with a Blake image. FAISS is a software library that indexes embeddings to retrieve the nearest matches to a query in milliseconds. Other metrics include: mAP (mean Average Precision), which measures whether the most relevant tags are ranked near the top of a multi-label prediction and NDCG (Normalised Discounted Cumulative Gain) which measures whether the most relevant retrieved images are ranked highest. None of these terms should obscure the operation they describe: convert each image into a numerical fingerprint, store the fingerprints in a fast lookup structure, and rank candidate matches for a scholar to verify.

Throughout Section 6, I use the following scholar-in-the-loop scenario as a concrete anchor. A researcher studying the serpent motif submits a query, either an image of the lower-left register of The Vision of the Last Judgement or the text string coiled serpent form. The system computes the query’s embedding, retrieves the 20 nearest works in the corpus, returns them ranked by similarity with provenance metadata (AI-suggested vs. human-validated; confidence; source tier), and the researcher confirms or rejects each match. The same example is used in 6.3 to describe the index, in 6.4 to demonstrate iterative taxonomy expansion, and in 6.5 to interpret the evaluation metrics.

div.head: 6.2 Methodological Framework
div.p: The methodological framework adopted in this paper uses pre-trained CLIP (ViT-B/32) in a zero-shot configuration, that is, without any fine-tuning on Blake-specific data. All similarity search, retrieval, and tag-candidate generation rely on CLIP’s original image–text embedding space. The discussion below of transfer learning, fine-tuning, few-shot learning, and supervised detection architectures (Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, ViT) is included to situate the chosen approach within the broader space of options and to clarify what trade-offs would attend a future fine-tuned or supervised variant; it does not describe the system evaluated in Sections 6.3–6.5. Zero-shot CLIP which was chosen because it permits flexible querying with natural-language tag prompts derived from Blake scholarship without requiring a labeled training set that the Archive does not currently provide.

A primary methodological approach involves leveraging transfer learning with powerful vision models pre-trained on large-scale image datasets . Models such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) or robust CNN architectures (e.g., ResNet families) serve as the starting point. The strategy involves fine-tuning these models on a curated dataset derived from the Archive .
Given the symbolic nature of Blake’s art, multimodal models like CLIP offer a particularly promising avenue :

list.item: Zero-Shot Tagging/Detection: Using a pre-trained CLIP model directly, without fine-tuning on Blake data. By providing textual prompts derived from art historical terms, CLIP can identify images or image regions that best match these descriptions. This allows for flexible querying and tagging based on semantic concepts.

Fine-tuning CLIP: Adapting a pre-trained CLIP model by fine-tuning it on image-description pairs extracted directly from the Archive . This would specialize the model to better understand the specific visual-semantic correlations present in Blake’s work.

Visual Similarity Search: Using CLIP embeddings to enable powerful visual similarity searches. Researchers could provide an image and find other visually similar instances across the archive or use a textual query to retrieve relevant images (radford_etal, 2021).

div.p: If creating a large, labeled dataset proves prohibitive, few-shot learning techniques offer a potential alternative . These methods are designed to enable models to learn and recognize new classes or concepts from only one or a very small number of examples. This could be particularly relevant for identifying rare but significant Blakean motifs or figures.

These methodologies collectively offer promising strategies for addressing the distinctive complexities of Blake’s visual art. Object detection and instance segmentation models provide a means of parsing Blake’s densely composed scenes by localizing individual figures and visual elements within crowded works such as The Vision of the Last Judgement . Multimodal approaches like CLIP further extend this capacity by linking visual patterns to textual descriptions, making them well suited for engaging with Blake’s symbolic and iconographic vocabulary . Transfer learning enables the development of detectors or classifiers attuned to Blake’s recurring motifs, capitalizing on visually consistent patterns that appear across his oeuvre . Finally, the robustness of models pre‑trained on large and diverse datasets supports their ability to accommodate the considerable stylistic variation evident across Blake’s output (he_etal, 2016).

table.head: Overview of Potential AI Models for Blake Analysis

div.p: The choice between these methodologies carries significant interpretive implications. An object detection approach inherently prioritizes the identification and localization of discrete visual elements. In contrast, using CLIP with textual prompts emphasizes semantic concepts as defined by language . The methodology selected will inevitably shape the kind of tags generated and, consequently, the type of scholarly analysis facilitated .

div.head: 6.3 Corpus Selection and Rationale
div.p: The implementation utilized a stratified corpus of 200 Blake works selected from 715 available in the William Blake Archive. This sample represents approximately 28% of the Archive’s holdings and was designed to balance representativeness with tractability for intensive methodological development.

list.item:
Genre diversity: The corpus was stratified proportionally across work types:
Illuminated manuscripts: 56 works (28%)
Drawings and paintings: 94 works (47%)
Commercial book illustrations: 30 works (15%)
Other (letters, notebooks, sketches): 20 works (10%)
Temporal range: Works span Blake’s entire career from 1779 to 1827, with deliberate inclusion of early (pre-1790), middle (1790-1810), and late (post-1810) periods to capture stylistic evolution.
Iconographic density: Priority given to works with multiple identifiable figures or complex compositional structures, as these provide richer test cases for motif detection.
The Archive description availability: Works with existing detailed the Archive descriptions were prioritized to enable text-image alignment experiments.

table.head: Corpus Composition by Work Type and Period

div.head: 6.3.2 What This Corpus Excludes and Why It Matters:
div.p: The selection strategy employed in this study necessarily introduces several forms of representational bias. Letters and prose manuscripts, for instance, remain underrepresented at 10% of the sample despite comprising approximately 14% of the Archive’s total holdings, largely because these materials lack the dense visual content central to the project’s analytical aims. Similarly, variant copies of illuminated books are collapsed into representative exemplars, such as selected versions of Songs of Innocence and of Experience or America a Prophecy, rather than including all extant copies (for example, all twenty-eight copies of Songs), a decision that privileges methodological tractability over comprehensive coverage. Commercial works, including the Night Thoughts engravings and the Virgil woodcuts, may also be proportionally underrepresented relative to their prominence within Blake’s broader output. Collectively, these omissions reflect deliberate methodological choices but also shape the resulting dataset in ways that must be acknowledged when interpreting the study’s findings. These choices optimize for methodological development, testing how well AI can handle Blake’s most visually complex works at the expense of statistical representativeness across his full output. A production system would require rebalancing toward the Archive’s actual distribution.

div.head: 6.4 Technical Implementation
div.p: Each work was processed using the OpenAI CLIP model (ViT-B/32) to generate 512-dimensional embeddings, capturing both visual features and semantic content through the model’s joint vision-language training (radford_etal, 2021). Processing confirmed correct dimensionality and L2 normalization — a mathematical transformation ensuring all embedding vectors have the same length (magnitude ≈ 1.0), which is required for meaningful similarity comparisons using cosine distance.

Integration into a FAISS index (Facebook AI Similarity Search, a library for efficient similarity search; specifically, IndexFlatIP, which computes exact inner-product similarity, equivalent to cosine similarity for normalized vectors, rather than approximate search) enabled sub-millisecond search latency (average 0.001 seconds per query) and high throughput (44,000+ queries per second) with low memory consumption (<100MB for the 200-work corpus). This architecture scales linearly: the full 715-work Archive would require approximately 280MB with proportionally maintained query performance .

To make the operation concrete: When our running scholar submits the textual query coiled serpent form, the system encodes the phrase with CLIP’s text encoder, queries the IndexFlatIP structure against the 200 image embeddings, and returns the top-k matches in well under a millisecond. The scholar sees a ranked list of works with thumbnails, similarity scores, and provenance flags, and can validate, override, or extend the suggestions in a single pass.

Semantic clustering validation demonstrated that the CLIP‑derived embeddings successfully capture semantically meaningful relationships across Blake’s visual corpus without requiring Blake‑specific fine‑tuning. Biblical works such as the Job illustrations and Divine Comedy designs consistently exhibited high cosine similarity scores (0.7–0.8), while mythological figures, including Urizen, Los, and Orc, formed coherent and distinct clusters within the embedding space. Figure 1 visualizes this clustering: a two-dimensional PCA projection of the 512-dimensional CLIP embeddings for the 200-work corpus, with markers colored by genre. Thematically related works cluster together without any Blake-specific fine-tuning, which both supports the use of CLIP as a retrieval backbone and previews the failure modes discussed in Section 7 (clusters reflect compositional and material similarity rather than iconographic meaning). Similarly, the model recognized the stylistic unity of Blake’s large color prints despite significant variation in subject matter, indicating sensitivity to formal rather than iconographic features. Notably, the various iterations of The Vision of the Last Judgement clustered tightly together regardless of differences in medium or date, underscoring the model’s ability to detect deeper compositional affinities that extend beyond material or historical contingencies.

A comprehensive web API was developed to demonstrate the system’s viability for production‑ready deployment, integrating a Flask framework with SQLAlchemy ORM to ensure modularity, efficient data management, and compatibility with existing digital humanities infrastructures. Designed to return JSON‑formatted responses containing similarity scores and associated metadata, the API maintains sub‑10ms response times for similarity queries, matching the performance requirements of real‑time exploratory research workflows. Stress testing further confirmed its robustness under concurrent load, with multiple simultaneous requests handled without degradation in throughput or latency, thereby establishing the architecture as sufficiently scalable for integration into larger archival ecosystems

div.head: 6.5 The Vision of the Last Judgement: Extended Case Study
div.p: To demonstrate the pipeline’s capabilities beyond whole-image similarity, a multi-layer analytical system focused on Blake’s The Vision of the Last Judgement was implemented. This experiment operationalizes art historical knowledge into successive computational passes.
Method Overview (with Incremental Passes):

list.item: Basic Pass: Heuristic identification of 6 canonical anchor figures (Christ, Satan, angels with trumpets, Book of Life, ascending souls, falling figures)
Enhanced Pass: Integration of expanded tag corpus yielding 112 enumerated visual/symbolic elements

Taxonomy Expansion: Incorporation of extended Blake mythology (581 entries from Damon’s Blake Dictionary), frequent characteristics (100), and judgment scene categories (10), producing 291 preliminary elements
Balancing & Confidence Profiling: Region distribution normalization plus weighted confidence model producing a refined set of 285 elements

div.p: The system draws on three primary categories of data assets that collectively enable its multi‑layered analytical process. First, the expanded taxonomy, comprising the blake_mythology_enhanced dataset with 581 terms, the frequent_blake_characteristics set of 100 recurrent visual features, and the judgment_scene_specific schema of 10 category groups, provides the semantic foundation for fine-grained motif and iconographic identification. Second, a layer of contextual intelligence, derived from spatial relationship frequencies and interpretive confidence distributions, provides the probabilistic structure necessary for weighting candidate identifications and modeling their interactions within Blake’s compositions. Finally, the region model, organized around seven compositional macro‑zones that mirror Blake’s vertical and soteriological axes as articulated by Billingsley (2018), furnishes the spatial framework through which detections are normalized and situated within the larger symbolic architecture of The Vision of the Last Judgement and related works.

table.head: Region Distribution Before vs. After Balancing

div.p: Weighted confidence (overall): 0.5637 (source weights: base 1.0; mythology 0.9; judgment categories 0.8; frequent characteristics 0.6; categorized tags 0.5). This enables comparative reliability scoring across iconographic strata.

The transition from undifferentiated tag lists to a regionally balanced, source‑weighted taxonomy enables a more methodologically rigorous representation of Blake’s compositions. This refinement corrects systemic statistical biases, most notably the disproportionate emphasis on throne-centered iconography, by redistributing interpretive attention across the full spatial and symbolic field of the work. In doing so, the model not only achieves a more equitable accounting of visual elements but also encodes key Blakean theological distinctives as machine‑interpretable features, thereby aligning computational outputs more closely with the interpretive frameworks articulated in Blake scholarship.

div.head: 6.5.1 Concrete Example: The Serpent in the Lower Register
div.p: The Basic Pass, using only canonical anchor figures, failed to identify the coiled serpent form in the lower-left region of The Vision of the Last Judgement. The system’s initial output associated this region with generic falling figures (confidence 0.62) — a pattern-level detection that missed the iconographically crucial identification of Satan wrapped in the Serpent’s coils.

The Enhanced Pass, incorporating the expanded Blake mythology taxonomy (581 terms including Satan-Serpent, Serpent of Error, coiled serpent form), successfully identified this element with Satan bound in serpent (confidence 0.71) appearing in the top-3 suggestions. Critically, the region-balancing step prevented this identification from being overwhelmed by the statistically dominant throne-region detections: Without balancing, the serpent identification ranked 47th overall; with balancing, it ranked 8th within its region and 12th overall.

This example illustrates both the potential and limits of the approach. The Enhanced Pass succeeded because serpent has consistent visual features (coiled form, scaled texture) that transfer from the model’s pre-training. But distinguishing Blake’s Serpent of Error from a generic serpent, understanding why this serpent embodies materialist philosophy in Blake’s cosmology, remains beyond the system’s capability. The AI provides the visual identification; the scholar provides the interpretive framework.

Returning to the running example: The same coiled serpent form query that succeeded at the whole-image level fails to localise the serpent within The Vision of the Last Judgement under the Basic Pass. The Enhanced Pass with the expanded taxonomy and regional decomposition described above correctly surfaces Satan bound in serpent in the top-3 suggestions for the lower-left region. This is the same outcome reported quantitatively below; the example here is meant to make the chain of operations (query → embedding → regional retrieval → ranked candidates → scholar validation) visible end to end.

Figure 2 (below) anchors the discussion: It shows the seven heuristic compositional zones used for region-balanced tagging: throne, upper heaven, judgment middle, resurrection field, lower corrective register, left ascension, and right descension, overlaid on Blake’s composition with the top detected interpretive elements per region.
