div.head: 6.6.1 Ground Truth Creation.
div.p: The evaluation dataset was developed through a two-phase process. First, the primary author (a doctoral researcher with expertise in both Blake scholarship and computer vision) generated initial annotations for the 200-work corpus, identifying visual elements using a structured taxonomy derived from Damon’s Blake Dictionary (1965) and Billingsley’s analysis of Blake’s visual vocabulary (2018). Second, these annotations were reviewed against the William Blake Archive’s existing scholarly descriptions to ensure alignment with established art-historical terminology. Disagreements between initial annotations and the Archive descriptions were resolved by defaulting to the Archive conventions, preserving consistency with the Archive’s editorial standards.

div.head: 6.6.2 Annotation Protocol Details
div.p: All annotations, taxonomy development, and manual verification were performed by the primary author, a doctoral researcher in digital humanities with four years of specialized training in Blake studies. The Expanded Taxonomy was derived from three primary sources:

list.item: The William Blake Archive’s existing illustration descriptions, ensuring alignment with established archival conventions; and
Northrop Frye’s Fearful Symmetry (1947) for thematic categories.

div.p: Terms were selected for inclusion if they (a) referred to visually identifiable elements rather than abstract concepts and (b) appeared in descriptions of at least three distinct Blake works in the Archive.

div.head: 6.6.3. Label Space Definition
div.p: The evaluation employed a hierarchical label taxonomy with three tiers:

list.item: Tier 1 (Object-level): 47 concrete visual elements (e.g., human figure, serpent, book, flames)
Tier 2 (Motif-level): 23 compositional and postural categories (e.g., outstretched arms, ascending figure, vortex composition)
Tier 3 (Iconographic-level): 15 Blake-specific identifications (e.g., Urizen, Los, Last Judgement scene)

div.p: This hierarchy reflects the distinction between pattern recognition (Tier 1), motif identification (Tier 2), and iconographic interpretation (Tier 3) discussed in Section 1.

div.head: 6.6.4 Evaluation Protocol
div.p: Given the pilot nature of this study, I employed a leave-one-out cross-validation approach for retrieval evaluation: each image was used as a query against the remaining 199 images, and retrieved results were evaluated against ground-truth similarity judgments. For tagging evaluation, I held out 40 works (20%) as a test set, using the remaining 160 for any fine-tuning experiments.

div.head: 6.6.5 Quantitative Results
div.p: Let’s discuss what the metrics measure, in terms of the running example. Top-1 accuracy asks whether the system’s single best suggestion for the serpent region is correct. Top-5 accuracy asks whether the correct identification appears anywhere in the top five candidates the scholar would see. mAP asks whether the correct candidates are ranked near the top across the full set of retrievals. NDCG asks whether the most relevant retrieved images outrank the less relevant ones. Read together, these metrics characterize the scholar’s experience of the interface, what they see first, and how much they have to scroll before reaching a usable match, rather than the system’s interpretive competence.
What does this mean?

list.item: Top-1 Accuracy measures how often the system’s single best prediction matches the ground truth. A Top-1 of 78.3% for object-level tags means that when the system suggests this image contains a serpent, it is correct approximately 4 out of 5 times.

Top-5 Accuracy measures whether the correct answer appears anywhere in the system’s top five suggestions. The 94.2% figure indicates that even when the system’s first guess is wrong, the correct object-level tag almost always appears within its top five candidates — useful for a human-in-the-loop workflow where scholars review suggested tags.

Mean Average Precision (mAP) captures both the accuracy and ranking quality of multi-label predictions. An mAP of 0.72 for object-level tags indicates that relevant tags tend to be ranked highly in the system’s output.

div.p: The declining performance from Tier 1 to Tier 3 reflects the expected increase in difficulty: detecting concrete objects is more tractable than identifying compositional motifs, which in turn is easier than making Blake-specific iconographic identifications. This gradient confirms that AI performs best on tasks closest to pattern recognition and struggles as tasks approach symbolic interpretation, a finding consistent with the theoretical framework established in Sections 1 and 3.

div.head: 6.6.6. Qualitative Evaluation.
div.p: Beyond quantitative metrics, I conducted a structured qualitative assessment following the protocol described in Appendix A.3. Twenty representative outputs were selected to span all three tagging tiers and multiple work types. The primary author, serving as the domain expert evaluator, rated each output without access to confidence scores using a three-point scale (Correct, Partially Correct, Incorrect) and provided written justifications for each rating.

Results of this assessment revealed a pattern consistent with the quantitative metrics: of the 20 evaluated outputs, 13 were rated Correct, 4 Partially Correct, and 3 Incorrect. Notably, all three Incorrect ratings occurred at the iconographic tier (Tier 3), while all object-level outputs (Tier 1) were rated Correct. The Partially Correct ratings typically involved cases where a visually accurate tag was interpretively incomplete — for instance, identifying bearded male figure where Urizen was the ground truth. Agreement between the qualitative ratings and quantitative confidence scores was moderate: outputs rated Correct had a mean confidence of 0.74, Partially Correct 0.58, and Incorrect 0.41.

For The Vision of the Last Judgement case study specifically, the Enhanced Pass correctly identified 5 of 6 canonical anchor figures (Christ enthroned, Satan, angels with trumpets, ascending souls, falling figures). The single misidentification, labeling a group of redeemed figures as apostles rather than Blake’s Four Zoas, illustrates the boundary between pattern recognition and iconographic interpretation precisely: The visual pattern (group of enthroned male figures) was correctly detected, but the Blake-specific mythological identification requires contextual knowledge the model lacks.

div.head: 6.6.7 Limitations
div.p: Five limitations bound the claims made above.

First, evaluation circularity. Where annotation disagreements arose during ground-truth construction, they were resolved by defaulting to the Archive’s descriptive conventions. The system is therefore being judged, in part, against a convention it is designed to align with. I do not present these results as validation against an external scholarly ground truth; I present them as a measure of alignment with the Archive’s established descriptive practice on a stratified sample. Future work should compare the system’s outputs against annotations drawn independently from Damon’s Blake Dictionary, from Frye and Mitchell’s critical traditions, and from non-Archive scholarly catalogs, so that the directions of agreement and disagreement can themselves be analyzed.

Second, single-annotator ground truth. All annotations, taxonomy decisions, and qualitative ratings in this pilot were produced by the primary author. Without inter-annotator comparison, I cannot report reliability statistics (Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α), and the Tier-3 numbers, which depend most heavily on contested iconographic judgments, are correspondingly more exposed to single-rater bias than the Tier-1 numbers. Mitigating this is properly the work of a follow-on study: Independent re-annotation of a stratified subsample by two or more Blake scholars, scored against the same three-tier label space, would yield both inter-annotator agreement and a system-vs-expert comparison. That work is out of scope for a feasibility pilot, but it is the natural next step before any of these numbers should be read as more than indicative.

Third, why 200 works is sufficient for the claims I make, and why it is not sufficient for the claims I do not make. A 200-work sample is adequate to estimate the relative performance gradient across the three tiers (Tier 1 > Tier 2 > Tier 3), to demonstrate sub-millisecond retrieval throughput on representative corpus volume, and to surface qualitative failure modes (e.g., blacksmith for Los, missed serpent under the Basic Pass). It is not adequate to estimate absolute accuracy at the level of the full Archive, to characterize rare iconographic types, or to support statistical generalization. The size was chosen to balance representativeness against the cost of intensive single-annotator work; it deliberately stops short of the corpus-wide claims that would require multi-annotator effort.

Fourth, the kind of Blake works likely to break the method. Three classes of work are most exposed. First, highly idiosyncratic compositions with rare or unique iconographic configurations. For example, certain plates of Jerusalem whose figural arrangements have few visual analogs in CLIP’s pre-training distribution will return weak top-k matches and unstable confidence scores. Second, densely overlapping symbolic scenes, such as crowd registers in the Last Judgement compositions, defeat whole-image retrieval because the dominant embedding signal is composition-level rather than figure-level; these require the regional decomposition introduced in Section 6.4 and remain difficult even then. Lastly, ambiguous or partially abraded figures, including faint pencil studies and damaged plates, produce embeddings dominated by material and tonal features rather than iconographic content, which surface as visually similar but iconographically unrelated retrievals.

Fifth, what would be required to claim generalization to the full Archive? Beyond hardware and storage scaling (which are inexpensive for 715 works at 512 dimensions), generalization claims require: a labelled evaluation subset stratified across the strata not yet sampled (especially manuscript marginalia and notebook content); multi-annotator agreement on at least Tier 2 and Tier 3; an external validation cohort of two to three Blake scholars unaffiliated with this study; and a separate held-out test set never seen during taxonomy construction. Until each of these is in place, the appropriate phrasing is performance on a 200-work stratified sample not performance on the Archive.

Finally, metrics like mAP and NDCG assess retrieval and ranking quality; they cannot assess whether a returned tag is interpretively meaningful to Blake scholars. The qualitative protocol described in Appendix A.3 partially addresses this for a 20-work subsample (13 Correct, 4 Partially Correct, 3 Incorrect, with all Incorrect ratings concentrated at Tier 3), but a more robust evaluation would require structured feedback from multiple independent domain experts under a pre-registered protocol.

div.head: 7. Critical Analysis: Mind the Gap Between AI and Humanistic Interpretation
div.p: A fundamental challenge lies in AI’s ability to handle the ambiguity and polysemy inherent in Blake’s work. Many of Blake’s symbols and figures carry multiple, often context-dependent, meanings . The serpent, for example, can represent error, materialism, energy, or even healing, depending on the specific work and its relation to Blake’s evolving thought . AI models, however, are typically trained to associate visual patterns with single, consistent labels. They struggle inherently with concepts that have fluid or multiple interpretations, often defaulting to the most statistically common association or failing to provide a confident prediction (spratt_etal, 2014).

There exists a significant gap between AI’s proficiency in recognizing literal visual patterns and the deeply symbolic, non-literal nature of Blake’s imagery. An AI might learn to detect the visual form of compasses. Still, it cannot inherently understand their symbolic weight as emblems of Urizenic reason, measurement, and the limitation of vision within Blake’s cosmology . Current AI lacks the world knowledge, cultural understanding, and reasoning capabilities to grasp allegory or complex personal mythologies .

It is crucial to distinguish between computational tagging, the identification and labeling of patterns based on learned correlations, and humanistic interpretation, the construction of meaning through critical engagement with the artwork within its historical, cultural, biographical, and theoretical contexts. AI can potentially automate aspects of description or visual analysis (finding motifs, identifying figures based on visual similarity). Still, it cannot perform the interpretive leap that characterizes scholarly understanding .

AI models are susceptible to biases present in their training data (drawford, 2021). identify a bias loop in cultural heritage ML pipelines: Biases embedded in historical collection practices (what was preserved, described, and prioritized) are encoded into training data, amplified by models, and then reintroduced into archival systems as seemingly objective outputs. This loop is particularly concerning for the Blake project, since the Archive descriptions reflect particular editorial judgments and historical schools of interpretation. If these are used for training, the AI may inadvertently learn and perpetuate those specific viewpoints while marginalizing alternative readings. Similarly, large pre-trained models like CLIP inherit biases from the vast web datasets they were trained on, which may include societal biases or skewed representations that could influence their analysis of Blake’s art in unforeseen ways (radford_etal, 2021). Our proposed integration architecture (Section 8) attempts to address this by maintaining provenance tracking and editorial separation between AI-generated and human-authored tags.

Evaluating AI performance in this context presents unique challenges (powers, 2011). Standard metrics like precision and recall measure the accuracy of pattern matching against a ground truth. Still, they cannot assess the interpretive quality or art historical relevance of the generated tags. How should an AI tag be evaluated if it correctly identifies a figure visually but misses its symbolic significance, or if it applies a label that is plausible but contested among scholars?

To complement the serpent identification success discussed in Section 6.4, consider an instructive failure: The system consistently tagged images containing Blake’s figure of Los with blacksmith (high confidence, 0.78) due to the anvil and hammer frequently depicted with this character. While visually accurate — Los is indeed depicted as a blacksmith — this tag is interpretively misleading. Los as blacksmith captures his craft but obscures his mythological significance as the embodiment of creative imagination and prophetic vision . A scholar encountering blacksmith in search results might overlook these images entirely when researching Blake’s mythology. This example illustrates why object-level tagging (Tier 1), even when accurate, cannot substitute for iconographic tagging (Tier 3) and why human oversight remains essential for interpretively meaningful discovery.

This typology suggests that the most concerning errors are not false positives (which human reviewers catch easily) but accurate but insufficient tags that correctly identify visual patterns while missing their interpretive significance.

Interestingly, the very limitations of AI when confronted with Blake’s art can possess heuristic value for scholars. When an AI model fails to confidently classify a section, produces contradictory tags for the same element across different contexts, or generates outputs that seem nonsensical to humans, it might not just signal a technical failure. Since AI models operate by identifying statistical patterns, their confusion can highlight areas where Blake’s work actively resists simple categorization or contains genuine ambiguity and symbolic complexity .

div.head: 8. Scholarly Implications: Advancing Blake Studies and Digital Humanities
div.p: The successful development of an AI-based tagging system for Blake’s works holds the potential to significantly enhance research methods within Blake studies. AI-generated tags, even if imperfect and requiring scholarly verification, could enable new forms of inquiry currently impractical at scale:

list.item: Large-Scale Iconographic Analysis: Researchers could track the frequency, distribution, and co-occurrence of specific figures, symbols, or motifs across Blake’s entire visual oeuvre as represented in the Archive, potentially revealing patterns in the evolution of his iconography or thematic concerns . The 200-work corpus already reveals that Los appears in 284 instances across 253 unique images, while Urizen appears in 94 instances — quantitative insights that would be difficult to derive manually.

Discovery of Visual Relationships: AI-powered visual similarity search could uncover previously unnoticed connections or variations between different works or details, suggesting avenues for comparative analysis .

Comparative Analysis of Versions: For works existing in multiple versions, like the illuminated books or the Last Judgement compositions, AI could assist in systematically comparing visual elements, potentially highlighting subtle but significant differences .

Text-Image Correlation: In the context of Blake’s illuminated books, AI analysis of visual elements could potentially be correlated with computational analysis of the accompanying text, enabling large-scale studies of Blake’s complex interplay between word and image

div.p: Enhanced visual tagging could substantially improve accessibility and discovery within the William Blake Archive. Currently, searching the archive often relies on knowing specific titles, keywords from textual descriptions, or browsing . An effective AI tagging system could enable users, both scholars and the general public, to search for images based on their visual content. This moves beyond metadata search towards content-based retrieval . Furthermore, AI-generated data could power new interfaces or visualizations, offering novel ways to explore Blake’s interconnected visual world.

This project is situated within the broader field of digital art history and contributes to its methodological advancement. Successfully applying advanced AI techniques to visual material as complex and symbolically dense as Blake’s art would represent a significant case study . It would push the boundaries of how AI is currently used in the humanities, moving beyond text analysis or simpler visual tasks towards engaging with core interpretive challenges. The methodological insights gained from preparing and utilizing the Archive data, particularly strategies for bridging the gap between scholarly description and AI data requirements, could offer valuable, reusable workflows for other projects working with similar cultural heritage data .

AI-driven analysis is unlikely to provide definitive interpretations, but it can be a powerful engine for generating new questions . Discovering unexpected correlations between motifs, observing shifts in the frequency of certain symbols over time, or finding visual similarities between seemingly unrelated works could prompt scholars to revisit existing interpretations or explore new hypotheses about Blake’s creative process, influences, or the development of his unique visual language (billingsley, 2018).

Pursuing this research necessitates careful attention to ethical considerations . Issues of representation, how AI models interpret and potentially simplify complex artworks, must be critically addressed. Transparency regarding the AI’s capabilities, its limitations, the data it was trained on, and potential biases is paramount . The goal should be augmentation, not replacement, of scholarly expertise.

The contribution of this paper is incomplete without a concrete account of how AI-suggested tags would coexist with human descriptive practice in an archive that has, for 30 years, prioritized scholarly objectivity and bibliographic rigor. I describe here the principles of representation, storage, and interface that follow from the three-tier framework and the limitations enumerated above. Together, they form an integration plan that other archives confronting dense symbolic corpora can adapt.

Each AI-generated annotation is represented as a structured record rather than a free-floating label. The record carries five fields: (1) a tier indicator distinguishing object-level, motif-level, and iconographic-level claims, with the tier setting the appropriate evidentiary burden; (2) a provenance field marking the tag as AI-suggested, human-validated, or human-overridden, with the validating scholar identified; (3) a confidence score on the [0,1] interval, reported alongside the source-weight tier used to compute it (base, mythology, judgment category, frequent characteristic, categorized tag); (4) a timestamp and version identifier covering both the model (e.g., CLIP ViT-B/32, OpenAI 2021) and the taxonomy snapshot under which the tag was produced, so that future re-runs can be compared against earlier states; and (5) a free-text justification or override note for any human-edited record.

row.cell: Sets the evidentiary burden for the tag; corresponds to the three-tier framework in Section 1.
Persistent: validation is additive, not erasing. Required for every record.
Reported alongside the source weight used to compute it.
Categorical (base / mythology / judgment category / frequent characteristic / categorized tag)
Encodes which taxonomy stratum contributed the tag.
Required for reproducibility and re-run comparison.
Identifies the taxonomy state under which the tag was generated.
Populated on validation or override. Identifies the responsible scholar.
Free-text justification when a scholar overrides an AI-suggested tag.

div.p: AI-suggested tags are stored as a separate annotation layer rather than written into the Archive’s authoritative descriptive metadata. This separation has three benefits: Human-authored descriptions remain editorially auditable in their current form; AI annotations can be re-generated wholesale when models or taxonomies are updated, without disturbing scholarly records; and queries can address the AI layer, the human layer, or their intersection. The annotation layer is queried via the same API surface as the retrieval prototype (Section 6.3) and is logged so that each tag has an immutable history of generation, validation, and override events.

Three interface principles follow from the foregoing. First, every AI-suggested tag is clearly marked as such in any user-facing view, with the marking persisting even after a scholar validates it (validation is additive, not erasing). Second, default filters in the Archive’s search and browse interfaces show validated-only results, with an opt-in toggle to surface AI-suggested tags as discovery aids. Third, every record exposes an audit trail accessible to authenticated users, so that scholarly reuse of AI-supported retrieval remains citable and contestable.

In keeping with the three-tier framework, success is intentionally modest. Success means improved discovery without substituting for interpretation; transparent provenance for every machine-generated claim; measurable improvement under human-in-the-loop review (validation rates, override rates, time-to-confirm); and the avoidance of interpretive foreclosure, that is, the system should expand rather than narrow the set of candidate readings a scholar considers. These criteria are specifically DH criteria: they prize archival integrity and scholarly agency over end-to-end automation.

div.head: 9. Conclusion: Contributions, Limitations, and Success Criteria
div.p: This pilot study offers three contributions at different levels of generality:

list.item: Conceptual framework: We articulate a hierarchy distinguishing pattern recognition, motif identification, and symbolic interpretation, clarifying where AI can assist and where human judgment remains essential. This framework, while developed for Blake, applies broadly to AI applications in iconographically complex art.

Functional prototype: We demonstrate that multimodal embeddings (CLIP) combined with efficient similarity indexing (FAISS) can achieve sub-millisecond retrieval across a 200-work Blake corpus with semantically meaningful results. Quantitative evaluation reveals a performance gradient, 78% Top-1 accuracy for object-level tagging, declining to 41% for iconographic identification, empirically confirming the theoretical distinction between pattern recognition and interpretation. The technical architecture is reproducible and adaptable to other digital art archives.

Methodological insights: The Vision of the Last Judgement case study reveals specific strategies, regional balancing, source-weighted confidence, iterative taxonomy expansion, for applying AI to densely symbolic compositions. The concrete example of serpent identification demonstrates both the potential (Enhanced Pass success) and limits (mythological interpretation remaining human) of these approaches.

div.p: This work has significant constraints that future research must address:

list.item: Scale: 200 works, while substantially larger than initial pilots, represents only 28% of the Archive’s 715 works and cannot establish statistical claims about Blake’s full corpus.
Annotation: Single-annotator ground truth limits reliability assessment; inter-annotator agreement studies are needed.
Evaluation: Quantitative metrics measure pattern-matching, not interpretive value to scholars.
Generalization: Performance on Blake may not transfer to artists with different visual vocabularies or to non-Western artistic traditions.
Temporal stability: CLIP and similar models evolve; results may vary with future model versions.

div.p: Beyond Blake, similar methodologies could address other artists known for personal iconography, Hieronymus Bosch, Odilon Redon, the Pre-Raphaelites, wherever dense symbolism challenges traditional cataloging.

I want to conclude here to be clear about what this pilot establishes, and what it does not. This pilot establishes three things: that multimodal embeddings combined with efficient similarity indexing can support sub-millisecond retrieval over a stratified Blake corpus; that performance degrades predictably across object-, motif-, and iconographic-level tagging, with the gradient itself a usable empirical finding for archives weighing adoption; and that the integration of AI tags into an existing scholarly archive can be operationalized concretely through provenance, confidence, version, and audit-log fields. It does not establish that the system interprets Blake, that its outputs generalize beyond the 200-work sample, or that the Tier-3 figures will hold under multi-annotator review. Read against the three-tier framework, success in this study has a specifically digital-humanities meaning: improved discovery without substituting for interpretation; transparent provenance for every machine-generated claim; measurable improvement under human-in-the-loop review; and the avoidance of interpretive foreclosure. AI here is a perceptual assistant under a scholar’s supervision, useful precisely because its limits are now mapped, not because they have been overcome.

div.head: Appendix A: Technical Implementation Details
div.p: Note: This appendix contains system architecture, performance benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.

div.head: A.1 System Architecture
div.p: The AI pipeline for analyzing Blake’s paintings consists of several integrated components designed for both research experimentation and production deployment. The architecture follows a modular design pattern enabling independent development and testing of each component.

list.item: Interfaces with the William Blake Archive API to retrieve images and metadata
Handles authentication, rate limiting, and data validation
Supports batch processing for large-scale corpus analysis
Image standardization: Resize to 224×224 pixels (CLIP ViT-B/32 requirement)
Normalization: ImageNet statistics (mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]) Format handling: Support for JPEG, PNG, TIFF formats
Metadata processing: XML parsing for TEI-encoded descriptions, text normalization
CLIP model: OpenAI ViT-B/32 architecture
Output: 512-dimensional normalized vectors
Batch processing: 32 images per batch for GPU efficiency
Storage: HDF5 format for efficient large-scale storage and retrieval
FAISS implementation: IndexFlatIP for cosine similarity
Metadata database: SQLite for development, PostgreSQL for production
Caching layer: Redis for frequently accessed embeddings
